list.listitem: Individuals who receive prenatal care during the first trimester have better pregnancy outcomes than those who receive little or no care. B
Early pregnancy confirmation and dating are important for improving pregnancy outcomes and allowing early risk modification. B
All pregnant persons, regardless of age, should be informed about prenatal genetic screening. C
All persons planning to or who could become pregnant should be on a daily folic acid supplement. A

Interventions that are effective in improving pregnancy outcomes include testing and treating sexually transmitted infections including human immunodeficiency virus, dietary counseling, daily folate supplementation, exercise, minimizing alcohol use, and smoking cessation. A

Universal screening for gestational diabetes and group B streptococcal colonization along with subsequent intervention if indicated are recommend in every pregnancy in the US. B Two-step screening for gestational diabetes appears optimal.
Early prenatal care (first trimester) with regularly scheduled follow-up visits can lead to healthier pregnancies and babies.

Prenatal care beginning in the first trimester declined from 78.3% in 2021 to 77% in 2022. The percentage of patients entering prenatal care in the third trimester or not receiving prenatal care in 2022 was 6.8%, an increase from 6.3% the previous year.
Individuals who receive prenatal care during the first trimester have better pregnancy outcomes than those who receive little or no care.
Prenatal care encompasses early and continuous risk assessment, health promotion, and medical and psychosocial interventions during pregnancy.
Common early symptoms include breast tenderness, amenorrhea, nausea, and fatigue.

Nausea and vomiting affects between 50-80% of pregnant patients and impacts quality of life, healthcare costs and missed work. Early effectivce management can avoid more severe complications such as hyperemesis gravidarum. First line non-pharmacologic treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy includes vitamin supplementation prior to pregnancy, dietary changes or oral ginger and lifestyle changes to avoid stimuli. First line pharmacolgic treatment includes varying doses and schedules of pyridoxine with or without doxylamine. Ondansetron is superior to metoclopramide in controlling vomiting, but similar for nausea. There is insufficient safety data in regard to ondansetron and the risk appears to be a small increase in risk of oral clefts associated with first trimester ondansetron exposure, thus starting after 10 weeks gestational age is best.

Signs of pregnancy include the following: Breast engorgement and areola darkening Linea nigra: hyperpigmented line extending from below the umbilicus toward the pubic symphysis. Chadwick’s sign: bluish discoloration of the cervix and vaginal tissue resulting from vascular engorgement. Goodell’s sign: softening of the cervix due to hormonal changes of early pregnancy.
Traditional scheduling of visits occurs: Monthly from diagnosis until 28 weeks gestation Twice monthly from 28 to 36 weeks gestation Weekly thereafter until delivery

In high-income countries, models of fewer visits (i.e. 8.2-12 encounters) do not increase risk to birthing parent or infant compared with the standard 13-visit model, and are expected to reduce overall costs. In moderate- to low-income countries, models of an abbreviated number of visits (many patients attending <5 encounters) were associated with significantly higher perinatal mortality (3 trials, RR 1.15; 95% CI, 1.01-1.32) compared with the standard 13-visit model. There were no clear differences between the groups for the other reported clinical outcomes. Patients in all settings are less satisfied with their prenatal care with fewer visits.
Antenatal care should be provided by a small group of caregivers who can provide continuity of care.

For low-risk pregnancies, midwife-led continuity models of prenatal care perform better than other models of pregnancy care with respect to fewer interventions (less regional analgesia, episiotomy and instrumental birth), higher rates of spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.05; 95% CI, 1.03-1.08), and fewer preterm births. Rates of Cesarean section were similar.

Early confirmation of pregnancy is essential to improve outcomes and permit early modification of risk factors. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends that gestational age (GA) and estimated due date (EDD) be determined and documented as early as possible from the last menstrual period (LMP), the first accurate ultrasound (US) examination, or both. Subsequent changes to the EDD should be reserved for rare circumstances. A GA and EDD that is not confirmed with early US (before 22 0/7 weeks) is considered "suboptimally dated”.
ACOG considers first-trimester ultrasonography to be the most accurate way to obtain GA and EDD.

ACOG provides guidance for managing pregnancies that are considered suboptimally dated, but notes that these women should be managed according to the same guidelines as patients with more accurate dating.
Naegele's rule can be used to calculate the EDD from the LMP. EDD = (First day of LMP − 3 months) + 7 days. The rule is most accurate in patients with regular 28-day cycles.

Ultrasound (US) before 14 weeks gestation is the most accurate method to establish or confirm EDD. First trimester US measurements of the gestational sac diameter or fetal crown rump length accurately confirm gestational age within ±5 to 7 days.For discrepancies between gestation age calculated by LMP and first trimester US, use .
Assess and document the body mass index (BMI) at the initial visit. Weight gain goals in pregnancy are based on pre-pregnancy BMI. See .

Patients with overweight or obesity have an increased risk of fetal, neonatal and infant death. Patients with a BMI of 30 have an absolute risk for fetal death of 102 per 10,000 pregnancies compared with 82 per 10,000 pregnancies for those with a BMI of 25 and 76 per 10,000 for those with a BMI of 20. Patients with obesity when they become pregnant are also at higher risk of antepartum and postpartum depression. Patients with obesity are also at an increased risk of cesarean delivery, failed trial of labor, endometritis, wound rupture or dehiscence, and venous thrombosis.
Patients with a prepregnancy BMI of less than 20 are at increased risk for preterm labor and SGA infants.

Blood pressure measurement is recommended at all prenatal visits. Although there is no evidence that regular screening decreases maternal or fetal morbidity or mortality, it is unlikely that a study will ever be done that withholds blood pressure measurement from a control group. Since this is simple, inexpensive, and acceptable to patients, screening is recommended empirically. BP levels over 140 mmHg systolic or 90 mmHg diastolic recorded on two occasions more than 6 hours apart indicate hypertension.

Examination of the breasts and nipples at the initial visit may detect breast lumps or the presence of inverted nipples. Routine breast examination during antenatal care is not recommended for promoting breastfeeding.
Routine pelvic examination does not predict preterm birth or cephalopelvic disproportion but may be helpful to identify individuals with female genital mutilation.

The goal of first trimester laboratory tests is for early detection of conditions that can adversely affect the pregnant patient or fetus during the pregnancy or may influence treatment should an adverse event occur.
Blood type, D (Rh) type, and routine antibody screening are recommended using Coombs’ testing. C

A complete blood count (CBC) is recommended in the first trimester. According to the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), there is insufficient evidence to assess the risk-to-benefit ratio of screening for iron deficiency anemia with a CBC or hemoglobin/hematocrit in pregnancy to prevent adverse maternal and birth outcomes.

Serum screen for rubella immunity should be done for all pregnant women at the initial prenatal visit. If the patient is found to be nonimmune, she should be counseled on the risks of congenital rubella syndrome and immunized after delivery. B
Routine screening for hepatitis B surface antigen is recommended by the USPSTF (2019) at the first prenatal visit. A

Universal screening for hepatitis C virus for every patient in each pregnancy is recommended by several organizations (2023) including the American Academy of Family Physicians; American College of Nurse-Midwives; American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists; Association of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses; National Association of Nurse Practitioners in Women’s Health; and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

Providers should ask patients about history of chicken pox infection or varicella immunization at the preconception or first prenatal visit. Consider varicella immunity testing if unsure history of infection or immunization to plan for prophylactic treatment if exposure to the varicella virus occurs during pregnancy.

Rapid plasma reagin or Venereal Disease Research Laboratory serologic testing should be done for syphilis. Confirmatory testing should be done using the more specific treponemal assay (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption). Pregnant patients with confirmed syphilis should be treated with penicillin G. B

Asymptomatic bacteriuria should be screened for using urine culture and sensitivity.A Urine dipstick is not recommended because it fails to identify group B streptococcus (GBS). If bacteriuria is present, antibiotics appear to reduce rates of pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low birthweight compared to placebo, but quality of evidence is low. A 7-day antibiotic regimen appears more effective than single dose regimens.

Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is strongly recommended at the first visit. Patients who test positive should be referred for treatment and counseling. A It is strongly recommended that patients at high risk for HIV (e.g.; those who inject drugs, have other STI during pregnancy, have multiple or new sex partners in pregnancy, incarceration in pregnancy, etc) be retested in the third trimester, preferably before 36 weeks gestation.

Gonorrhea and chlamydia screening are recommended for all patients at the intial appointment. Patients who test positive should be treated and a test of cure should be done. B A single dose of 500 mg IM ceftriaxone is recommended as first-line therapy for gonorrhea and single 1 gram dose of azithromycin is recommended for chlamydia. Amoxicillin or erythromycin are both acceptable alternatives for genital chlamydial infections in pregnancy if there is drug intolerance or a contraindication to first-line therapy.
Cervical cancer screening should be performed during the pregnancy if the patient is due for testing according to the ASCCP guidelines. A
Although not routine, first trimester testing for cytomegalovirus and treatment with valacylovir has been proposed, and models suggest it would be cost-effective if implemented.
During the first trimester, pregnant women have additional caloric requirements of 150 calories per day; this increases to 300 to 500 extra calories per day in the second and third trimester.

Dietary advice may reduce the risk of developing gestational diabetes mellitus (5 trials, low-quality evidence) and possibly the risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension (2 trials, low-quality evidence).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 117 studies with 34,546 participants found that antenatal structured diet and physical activity–based lifestyle interventions were associated with a reduction in gestational weight gain (-1.15 kg; 95% CI -1.4 to -0.91) and lower risk of gestational diabetes (OR 0.79; 95% CI 0.70 - 0.89). Diet interventions compared with control were also associated with reduced neonatal intensive care admissions (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.48 - 0.95), large-for-gestational-age neonate (OR 0.19; 95% CI 0.08 - 0.47), and total adverse neonatal outcomes (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.26 - 0.72). Risk of bias in this literature, however, was high.

A 2025 meta-analysis found that few trials explore physical activity in pregnancy are high-quality, and those that are high-quality did not find an association between activity and pregnancy or birth outcomes.
Vegan-vegetarian diets during pregnancy are not associated with an increase in severe adverse outcomes or major malformations; the influence on infant birth weight is conflicting.
Salt restriction does not appear to prevent preeclampsia.

Mercury can have an adverse effects on fetal neurologic function. Pregnant patients should not eat swordfish, shark, king mackerel or tilefish because they contain high levels of mercury; pregnant patients should also pay attention to local fish advisories. The FDA recommends that pregnant patients not consume more than 12 ounces of tuna per week.

Patients should be counselled to wash hands prior to touching food, thoroughly cook all meats, wash all fruits and vegetables prior to consumption, avoid cat feces in litter boxes or soil, and wear gloves when gardening to avoid toxoplasmosis exposure. C Routine serologic screening for toxoplasmosis is not advised because harms from screening outweigh benefits. B

Patients should be counseled to drink only pasteurized milk and avoid soft cheeses such as brie and camembert as a means to avoid listeriosis. Pate and undercooked meats, including cold cuts, should be avoided. C
Salmonella infection risk can be reduced by avoiding contact with or ingestion of raw or partially cooked eggs or meat, especially poultry.

Caffeine use less than 200 mg does not appear to be a major contributing factor in miscarriage and preterm birth according to a 2010 ACOG Committee opinion. However, high-quality evidence is lacking on the effects of caffeine use during and before pregnancy. Low levels of caffeine use appear to be safe and there is no evidence to support the further restriction of caffeine below 200 mg/day. A retrospective cohort analysis did show even small amounts of caffeine use were associated with smaller child height beginning at age 4 years and persisting to age 8 years.

Folic acid: The USPSTF (2023) recommends a daily supplement of 0.4 mg to 0.8 mg folic acid for all persons who plan to or could become pregnant; the critical period for prevention of NTDs starts at least 1 month before conception and continues through the first 2-3 months of pregnancy. The USPSTF also recommends that pregnant persons without a history of NTDs take 0.4-0.8 mg of folic acid supplementation daily. The CDC recommends that patients who have delivered a child with an open NTD should consume 4 mg of folate one month prior to pregnancy and during the first trimester. Consuming 400 μg of folate daily prior to conception and during the first trimester of pregnancy reduces the risk of having a fetus with a neural tube defect (NTD), but has no clear benefit on reducing other birth defects. A Authors of a systematic review of 24 studies found consistent evidence from pre-fortification studies of a protective effect for NTD, including the single RCT, with OR ranging from 0.11 to 0.7, but no benefit from more recent case-control studies.A Patients who take folic acid prior to conception also have a reduced risk of giving birth to infants who are small for gestational age (<10th percentile).

Iron supplementation is not indicated routinely in pregnancy. A The USPSTF found insufficient evidence that routine prenatal iron supplementation improves maternal or infant clinical health outcomes; supplementation may improve maternal hematologic indices. If iron supplementation is used, intermittent regimens produce similar maternal and infant outcomes as daily supplementation, and are associated with fewer side effects.

Fish oil: Limited evidence supports the use of fish oil taken during pregnancy to reduce the rates of wheezing disorders in children younger than 5 years. In a RCT of 695 Danish women who took 4 capsules of 1 g fish oil daily the number needed to treat (NNT) was 14.6. Limited evidences also supports maternal fish oil supplementation to reduce allergies in children.

There is mixed evidence for the benefit of calcium supplementation to reduce the risk of hypertensive disorders. Calcium supplementation (at least 1 g daily) may reduce the risk of high blood pressure (RR 0.65; 95% CI, 0.53-0.81) and preeclampsia (RR 0.45; 95% CI, 0.31-0.65), especially for patients with low baseline calcium intake. Benefit may be overestimated due to heterogeneity between studies and possible publication bias. In a sensitivity analysis of 13 meta-analyses including 15,730 participants, authors added studies stepwise, starting with the largest sample size, to assess the influence of the smaller studies. These authors found that the 3 largest studies with 13,815 participants (88%) showed a RR of 0.92 (95% CI 0.80 - 1.06; NS) and no evidence of heterogeneity. Only when the smaller studies were included, did the results show benefit. Calcium supplementation does not appear beneficial in the prevention of preterm birth or low infant birth weight.
Multiple-micronutrient supplementation with iron and folic acid reduces the risk of low birthweight and likely reduces preterm birth.

Vitamin D supplementation may reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia, low birth weight and preterm birth; however, combined vitamin D and calcium appear to increase the risk of preterm birth. Therefore, it is not known whether vitamin D supplementation should be part of routine antenatal care for all patients to improve maternal and infant outcomes. The addition of prenatal vitamin D does not reduce the risk of asthma in children up to age 6 years.

Vitamin A intake over 700 μg daily should be avoided because of possible teratogenicity. Liver and liver products also contain high amounts of vitamin A and are best avoided during pregnancy. Vitamin A supplementation does not appear to reduce maternal or perinatal mortality; however, in populations deficient in vitamin A or in women with HIV, supplementation with vitamin A reduces maternal anemia and maternal night blindness.

Zinc supplementation: There is evidence of a reduction in preterm birth for zinc compared with placebo, primarily for pregnant patients of low income, but no evidence of other benefits during pregnancy.
Other vitamins: There is insufficient evidence to support routine supplementation with vitamin B6, C, D, or E or magnesium during pregnancy.

Probiotic supplementation in pregnancy does not protect against subsequent wheezing or asthma in children at 2 to 6 years of age. A 2025 randomized trial found it also did not prevent eczema or food allergies in offspring at 1 year of life. This contradicts an earlier (2016) meta-analysis that found probiotic supplementation both prenatally and postnatally appeared to reduce risk of atopy (RR 0.78; 95% CI, 0.66-0.92).
Suggested pregnancy weight gain is 28-40 pounds for underweight patients, 25 to 35 pounds for normal-weight patients and 15-25 pounds for overweight patients (See Table 4).

Antenatal nutritional education to increase energy and protein intake in the general obstetric population appears to be effective in reducing the risk of preterm birth, low birthweight, and increasing birthweight among undernourished women.

Diet or exercise, or both, during pregnancy reduce the risk of excessive gestational weight gain based on high-quality evidence from a 2015 Cochrane Review. The risk of maternal hypertension and cesarean delivery, macrosomnia, and neonatal respiratory morbidity appear to be reduced as well, particularly for high-risk patients receiving combined diet and exercise interventions.

Authors of one RCT found a combination of community-based exercise sessions, home exercise instruction, and dietary counseling for pregnant patients between 20 weeks and 36 weeks of gestation reduced the prevalence of excessive gestational weight gain (35% vs. 55%; NNT = 2.5).

In a meta-analysis of interventions to limit excessive gestational weight gain, the provision of information, motivational interviewing, behavioral self-monitoring and providing rewards contingent on successful behavior were helpful strategies. In one RCT, the use of weight-gain education, a personalized weight graph, formalized exercise prescription and regular monitoring did not reduce the number of patients exceeding recommended weight gain but did lower mean gestational weight gain (14.2 kg [SD 4.4] vs. 15.3 kg [SD 5.4] in the control group).
A meta-analysis of 9 trials of dietary or exercise interventions for patients with obesity did not find any improvements in maternal or newborn outcomes.

Advise patients to abstain from drinking alcohol or limit alcohol to no more than one standard unit daily. One unit of alcohol equates to one small glass of wine, one half pint of beer, or one shot. Since the minimal amount of alcohol exposure that results in fetal alcohol syndrome is unknown, many consensus statements recommend abstinence from all alcohol during pregnancy.

One large British prospective study of 9460 households found no increase in cognitive or behavioral problems in young children whose mothers engaged in light drinking (1-2 drinks per week) during pregnancy (29% of the population).

Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to recommend the use of home visits for pregnant patients with a drug or alcohol problem for reducing alcohol consumption or increasing breast feeding.

Patients who are survivors of intimate partner violence should be evaluated for immediate safety and provided information about safe houses; in one RCT, cognitive behavioral therapy (including information about abuse and violence, a danger assessment, and prevention options) delivered during pregnancy reduced the recurrence of self-reported violence episodes.

Social support for patients during pregnancy while unlikely to prevent low birthweight or preterm delivery appears helpful in reducing the likelihood of antenatal hospital admission and cesarean birth.
Sexual intercourse during pregnancy is not associated with any adverse outcomes in an otherwise healthy pregnancy.

Hot tub use has been associated with a small increased risk of neural tube defects and may be associated with an increase in anencephaly and gastroschisis. Pregnant patients should be counseled to avoid hot tub use and limit to 10 minutes or less if one is used.
Routine dental care is safe and important to the health of pregnant patients. Elective dental work is ideally timed for the second trimester, but emergent work may be performed at any time.

Pregnant patients should be counseled about the correct use of seat belts. Three-point harnesses should be used whenever the patient is driving or riding. The shoulder belt should be worn between the breasts and the lap belt positioned over the hips.
Long airline flights are associated with an increased risk of venous thrombosis; whether the risk increases in pregnancy is unclear. The use of compression stockings may decrease risk.
Attending childbirth education classes was associated with a vaginal delivery in a retrospective study of 14,630 pregnant patients.

Cochrane authors failed to find conclusive evidence supporting prenatal education for improving initiation, duration, or proportion of patients providing any or exclusive breastfeeding at three or six months. The USPSTF, however, recommends education and support that encourages breastfeeding both during pregnancy and after birth, while respecting a patient’s autonomy.

Beginning or continuing a moderate routine of exercise during pregnancy is not associated with adverse outcomes. Regular aerobic exercise during pregnancy improves (or maintains) physical fitness, but data are insufficient regarding risks or benefits for the mother or infant.

In an RCT of 840 Spanish pregnant patients, those who participated in a supervised exercise program of three 50- to 55-minute sessions weekly from late first trimester until term were less likely to develop hypertension (2.1% vs. 5.7%) or gestational diabetes (2.4% vs. 5.5%), to gain excess weight (26% vs. 34%), or to give birth to a macrosomic infant (1.8% vs. 4.7%) than individuals receiving standard care.

Authors of a meta-analysis also found that moderate physical exercise decreased GDM risk as well as decreasing maternal weight gain among otherwise healthy sedentary individuals. Most beneficial were programs that were continuous throughout pregnancy and those that combined aerobic exercise with resistance or strength training.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 RCTs found a reduced risk of cesarean delivery of 14.2% with an exercise intervention vs. 17.8% for controls; RR 0.85; 95% CI, 0.73-0.99; NNT = 33).

In the most recent meta-analysis of exercise trials, physical activity interventions were associated with a lower risk of gestational diabetes (OR 0.60; 95% CI 47 - 0.75), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (OR 0.66; 95% CI 0.48 - 0.90), cesarean delivery (OR 0.85; 95% CI 0.75 - 0.95), and total adverse maternal outcomes (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.71 - 0.86).
Low-moderate quality evidence supports land-based exercise for reductions in pregnancy-related low back pain, disability, and sick leave more than usual prenatal care.
Exercise may be effective in treating depression during pregnancy.
Contact sports, high-impact or high-velocity sports, scuba diving, and aggressive racquet sports are best avoided during pregnancy. C

section.type: Smoking, recreational drug use and occupational exposures
section.heading: Smoking, recreational drug use and occupational exposures

list.listitem: Smoking during pregnancy contributes to adverse outcomes like low birth weight and preterm delivery. Quitting at any stage of pregnancy confers benefit. Patients who cannot quit smoking should be counseled to reduce the number of cigarettes smoked. Interventions that might help reduce smoking during pregnancy include physician advice, behavioral modification, and group sessions; however, a meta-analysis found no important benefit of smoking cessation counseling on quit rates during pregnancy.

Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found that psychosocial interventions, in particular counseling, feedback and incentives, to support patients to stop smoking in pregnancy can increase the proportion of patients who stop smoking in late pregnancy (RR 1.44; 95% CI, 1.19-1.73) and the proportion of infants born low birthweight (mean difference 55.60 g; 95% CI, 29.82-81.38 g higher).

Three RCTs comparing nicotine patches with placebo, brief smoking intervention, or usual care failed to demonstrate that nicotine patches significantly affected cessation rates. Cochrane authors found benefit from nicotine replacement on smoking cessation rates but not when only high-quality trials were considered. Only one trial demonstrated a positive effect on developmental outcomes in newborns so more research is needed. The safety of nicotine replacement therapy during pregnancy is not established. B

In a small pilot RCT, pregnant patients smokers randomized to twice daily 150 mg bupropion sustained release vs. placebo for 12 weeks had significantly higher abstinence rates during treatment (19% vs. 2%), although no longer significant by treatment end (17% vs. 3%) or at the end of pregnancy (10% vs. 3%).

Recreational drug use should be discouraged and any drugs consumed reviewed for safety during pregnancy. Patients should be informed that cannabis exposure is associated with low birthweight (adjusted OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1 - 1.3) and small-for-gestational age (aOR 1.2, 1.18 - 1.3) infants with a dose-response gradient. In one community hospital experiencing an increase in neonatal abstinence syndrome, universal maternal urine drug screening resulted in an additional 19 patients being detected with opioid use who had no screening risk factors—20% of the 96 patients with positive screens. Psychosocial interventions for pregnant patients enrolled in illicit drug treatment programs, however, did not improve retention or abstinence and were also not effective in reducing preterm birth rates or low birth weight.

Combination buprenorphine and naloxone is safe and may be a more effective treatment option compared with buprenorphine alone for opioid-use disorder in pregnancy. In this study using data from Medicaid-insured pregnant individuals from 2000 to 2018 comparing 3369 patients who received combination buprenorphine/naloxone during the first trimester with 5326 patients who received buprenorphine alone or switched from the combination to buprenorphine alone, the former group had a significantly reduced risk of the neonatal abstinence syndrome (37.4% vs 55.8%; NNT = 5.4, 4.6 - 6.6) and neonatal intensive care admission (30.6% vs 34.9%; NNT = 23.0, 15.7 - 43.0).

A 2025 study found that use of buprenorphine before and throughout pregnancy was associated with a higher likelihood of continuing use after pregnancy. Patients who discontinued use of buprenorphine during pregnancy or who initiated it during pregnancy had a higher rate of non-fatal overdose compared with patients who used it continuously before and throughout pregnancy. The use of buprenorphine did not affect the rate of neonatal abstinence syndrome.

Occupational and environmental exposures should be minimized, such as exposure to solvents (e.g., pesticides, paint thinner/strippers, fertilizers), heavy metals (e.g., lead, mercury or arsenic), anesthetic gases (which may reduce fertility in settings where gas-scavenging equipment is not available), and ionizing radiation.

In one prospective study of 1,505 mother-infant pairs in rural Bangladesh, there were negative effects on children's growth at age 5 years attributable to prenatal and early-life arsenic and cadmium exposure.

In a study of maternal exposure to air pollution, increased concentrations of particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter smaller than 10 μm were associated with multiple congenital heart defects (adjusted OR 1.05; 95% CI, 1.01-1.10).

Few medications or complementary and alternative therapies are proven safe during pregnancy due to lack of evidence. Prescription and nonpresecription medications should be used only if absolutely necessary. C Meta-analysis of 29 cohort studies of women who used SSRIs during the first trimester reveals a generally small risk of congenital malformations and argues against a substantial teratogenic effect of SSRIs.

One database study found that 14.4% of US patients were dispensed an opioid at some point during pregnancy despite limited safety data. However, in a Korean national database study of over 3 million children born over an 8-year period, 7% of whom were exposed to prenatal opioids, authors found no evidence of increased risk of neuropsychiatric disorders associated with opioid use when controlling for rates among unexposed siblings.
A Swedish national cohort study found no increased risk of neuropsychiatric disorders in the offspring of pregnant parents who took acetaminophen during pregnancy.

In a US database study, exposure to amphetamine/dextroamphetamine or methylphenidate exposure during pregnancy did not appear to increase the risk of childhood neurodevelopment disorders in children at least 2 years of age.

Vaccinations that can be given routinely during pregnancy include influenza, COVID, and RSV and Tdap (ideally provided between 27–36 weeks' gestation). In a Canadian cohort study of 31,295 children exposed to the 2009 pandemic H1N1 influenza vaccination in utero, there was no association between vaccination and subsequent illness in the exposed children over the first 5 years of life.

Perinatal immunization with Tdap protects both the pregnant person and the offspring and results in high concentrations of pertussis antibodies in infants during the first 2 months of life. Administration of Tdap to pregnant persons with recent (<5 years) prior tetanus immunizations does not increase adverse vaccine effects. Safety for the fetus was confirmed in a systematic review of 21 studies of antenatal combined Tdap administration during the second or third trimester of pregnancy.

BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy is not associated with adverse neonatal outcomes including preterm birth, rate of small for gestational age, or neonatal hospitalizations based on data from 16,697 newborns were exposed in utero and followed up to 6 months of age.
A bivalent RSV vaccine given to pregnant patients between 24 and 36 weeks' gestation safely reduces the likelihood of severe RSV in their newborns (NNT = 81 at 6 months of age).

Other vaccines that can be provided if indicated during pregnancy include hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal and pneumococcal. Others should be administered before or after pregnancy (see CDC Summary of Maternal Immunizations Recommendations). There are no data, however, on the benefit of hepatitis B vaccine during pregnancy for preventing infant infection.
All pregnant patients, regardless of age, should be informed about prenatal genetic screening.
Carrier screening is genetic testing on an individual who does not exhibit any specific phenotype but may carry genetic alleles associated with a diagnosis.
All pregnant patients should be provided counseling for carrier screening.
Carrier counseling and screrning should ideally be performed before pregnancy and should only need to be performed once in a lifetime.

If a patient tests positive as a carrier, the reproductive partner should also be offered carrier screening. If both test positive, they should be referred to a genetic counselor for further discussion and testing.

Carrier screens are recommended for all patients with spinal muscular atrophy and cystic fibrosis. Targeted carrier screens are recommended for patients with hemoglobinopathies, fragile x syndrome, Eastern and Central European Jewish descent, and Tay-Sachs disease but can also be offered regardless of race or ethnicity in expanded carrier screening.
Fetal Aneuploidy Screening is screening for abnormal number of chromosomes of the fetus during a pregnancy
Risk of fetal aneuploidy increases with maternal age but can occur in any patient of any race or ethnicity.
Down's syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most common non sex-chromosome-linked aneuploidy and occurs in 1 in 700 live births.
Screening tests for aneuploidy are currently available in any trimester and options are shown in .

For patients who are late in attending prenatal care, later screening at 18 to 35 + 6 weeks gestation for aneuploidy using alpha-fetoprotein and B-hCG had similar detection and false positive rates as screening between 14 to 17 + 6 gestation.

Cell-free DNA has the highest detection rates for Trisomy 21 and can also be used to detect fetal sex and Rh(+) fetus in an Rh(-) pregnant patient as well as some other paternally-derived autosomal-dominant abnormalities. False positive rates are higher in low-risk patients.

Ultrasonography of the fetal nuchal translucency or nasal bones alone can be used as a first trimester marker for aneuploidy (specifically in multiple gestations) as well as Noonan Syndrome, cardiac malformations, skeletal dyplasias and other anatomic anomalies.
Intended to determine, with as much certainty as possible, whether a specific fetal chromosomal abnormality is present.

Fetal cells for genetic testing can be obtained from amniotic fluid by amniocentesis, placental tissue by chorionic villus sampling (CVS), or fetal blood - though fetal blood and tissue are rarely required for prenatal diagnosis and thus cord blood sampling or fetal tissue biopsy are rarely used for this indication.

CVS is generally performed between 10 to 13 weeks gestation through ultrasonographic guided transcervical or transabdominal route. Specimen processing time is 5-7 days. Pregnancy loss rate has decreased over time and is currently ˜0.22% (1 in 455) and incidence of vaginal spotting after transcervical sampling is 32% (lower in transabdominal route).

Amniocentesis is generally performed between 15 to 20 weeks gestation but can be performed at any later GA. Specimen processing time is 7 to 14 days. Pregnancy loss rate is somewhat lower than CVS sampling (0.11%). Complication rates for both techniques are dependent on expertise of the sampling provider.

Ultrasonography is used to obtain accurate pregnancy dating, prenatal genetic screening (Nuchal Translucency) and diagnosis (US guided testing), evaluation of fetal anatomy, monitoring of fetal growth and development, detection of placental misplacement (placental previa) or invasion (placental accreta) as well as evaluation for fetal distress with umbilical artery Doppler US and the biophysical profile (BPP) in high-risk pregnancies.
A standard ultrasound will give the following information in pregnancy: pregnancy location, fetal number, cardiac activity, fetal biometry, placental location, and amniotic fluid volume.
The quality of each ultrasound is dependent upon the sonographer's experience and equipment and further evaluation and managment must take this into consideration.

An ultrasound is typically performed around 20 weeks gestation to evaluate fetal anatomy and screen for fetal anomalies. Additional ultrasounds are recommended in the second and third trimesters for the following: suspected amniotic fluid abnormalities, suspected placental abruption, evaluation of prelabor rupture of membranes or premature labor, evaluation of abnormal biochemical markers, follow-up evaluation of placental location for suspected placenta previa, and suspected fetal death.

ACOG recommends all pregnant women be offered ultrasonographic evaluation in pregnancy. However, in the only RCT of routine ultrasound conducted in 15,151 pregnant women at low risk for perinatal problems and performed at 15 to 22 weeks' gestation and again at 31 to 35 weeks, ultrasound was not associated with improved perinatal outcomes; adverse perinatal outcome occurred in 5% percent of the women in the ultrasound-screening group and 4.9% among the infants of the women in the control group. Routine late pregnancy ultrasound, defined as greater than 24 weeks' gestation, in women with either unselected or low-risk pregnancies, including those who had an initial ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation, is also not associated with benefits for mother or baby.

Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a condition that develops during pregnancy in which the mother becomes glucose intolerant; GDM generally resolves after delivery. GDM is associated with multiple maternal and perinatal complications including preeclampsia, higher risk of cesarean section, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma and stillbirth.
A1GDM refers to diet-controlled GDM.
A2GDM refers to medication-controlled GDM (oral or insulin).
From 2012 and 2016, GDM was reported in around 6% of pregnancies in the US.
There is an increased incidence of GDM in patients of African American, Hispanic American, Native Americans, Pacific Islander, and South or East Asian race/ethnicity compared to white women.
Universal GDM screening is recommended after 24 weeks gestation by USPSTF, ACOG and the American Diabetes Association (ADA). Screening is generally performed between GA 24-28 weeks.

Screening before 24 weeks is recommended in certain high risk individuals including obesity (BMI >30 kg/m2), high risk racial or ethnic group, first degree relative with Type 2 DM, previous infant with birth weight over 4,000 gm (9 lbs), history of hypertension or prediabetes, or history of polycystic ovarian syndrome.

In an RCT including 802 pregnant patients with one or more risk factors for GDM, early screening (before 20 weeks' gestation) with immediate treatment for those testing positive for GDM vs. delayed treatment (24-28 week following repeat testing) resulted in decreased rate of a composite of adverse neonatal outcomes (24.9% vs. 30.5%; adjusted RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7 - 0.98; NNT = 18). Maternal outcomes did not differ between groups.

Screening is performed with either a one-step or two-step approach. The two-step approach is the most commonly used and consists of a 50 gram glucose drink followed by a 1-hour serum glucose. If this value is greater than the institutional cutoff (usually 130-140 mg/dL), a 100-gram glucose drink will be administered with serum glucose testing at 1, 2, and 3 hours. If two of these values are elevated, the patient meets criteria for GDM. The one-step approach consists of a fasting serum glucose followed by a 75 g oral glucose solution followed by a serum glucose check at 1 hour and 2 hours. One elevated glucose reading qualifies for a diagnosis of GDM.

Multiple RCTs have been conducted to determine differences in outcomes between one-step and two-step testing. There has been no statistical difference in primary outcomes between the two groups, including large for gestational age infants. However, the one-step testing was associated with higher rates of GDM diagnosis and treatment, NICU admission and neonatal hypoglycemia.

Cochrane authors found insufficient evidence to determine which test (75 g vs. 100 g glucose load, candy bar vs. 50 g glucose monomer drink, 50 g glucose polymer or food load vs. monomer drink), test strategy (one vs. two-step) or diagnostic criteria (World Health Organization vs. American Diabetes Association) was best for diagnosis of GDM.
The general recommendation is for glucose monitoring four times daily, one fasting and three postprandial measurements.
The ADA and ACOG recommend fasting glucose levels <95 mg/dL, 1 hour PP <140 mg/dL, and 2 hour PP <120 mg/dL.

First-line treatment includes lifestyle modification counseling: diet modification, exercise (30 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise at least 5 days a week) and self-glucose monitoring. A low-glycemic index diet failed to improve outcomes in one RCT.

Authors of a 2017 meta-analysis concluded that lifestyle intervention was associated with lower rates of postnatal depression and increase likelihood of reaching post pregnancy goal weight reduction. Additionally, infants born to mothers with GDM who received lifestyle modification counseling were less likely to be large for gestational age or macrosomic.

A 2025 trial enrolled 167 participants at risk of GDM and randomized them to time-restricted eating (intermittent fasting) and exercise or a control group. It followed the 111 participants who ultimately became pregnant and compared rates of GDM onset as measured by 2 hour GTT, but found no differences.

There is no conclusive evidence for when medical therapy should be started. It is reasonable to start medications if there is consistent hyperglycemia with fasting glucose >95 mg/dL, 1 hour postprandial >140 mg/dL, and/or 2 hour postprandial >120 mg/dL.

Insulin is the preferred first-line medication. Insulin does not cross the placenta. The typical starting dose is 0.7 to 1.0 units/kg daily divided into long-acting or intermediate-acting plus short-acting insulin. If there are isolated abnormal values at a certain time of the day, insulin therapy can be focused around that time.

Despite not being FDA approved, metformin has been used for GDM. It is appropriate for women who are unable to safely administer insulin, cannot afford insulin, or decline to use insulin therapy. Dosage starts at 500 mg per night for 1 week and is increased to 500 mg twice daily. The maximum daily dose is 2500 to 3000 mg daily in 2-3 divided doses. Metformin does cross the placenta and has been shown to be present in fetal concentrations as high as maternal concentrations. There are no long-term safety data for metformin use in pregnancy, so patients should be counseled on this. One recent study showed similar developmental outcomes in offspring at 2 years of age.

Glyburide is also not FDA approved and is infrequently used. It also crosses the placenta. The dose is 2.5 to 20 mg divided into multiple doses. Four to 16% of women will require additional insulin to obtain good glucose control. Previous meta-analyses have shown increased rates of macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, preeclampsia, hyperbilirubinemia, and stillbirth compared with insulin.
Antenatal testing is recommended for all women with gestational diabetes with poor glycemic control or who require any medication intervention. Testing should begin at 32 weeks GA.

The specific type of testing and frequency is according to local practice. Studies have not shown an increase in stillbirth in those with well-controlled A1GDM before 40 weeks so antepartum fetal testing may not be necessary. There is no consensus about antenatal testing in A1GDM.

list.listitem: Obtaining repeat weights during prenatal care can be limited to situations where clinical management is likely to be influenced by these data.
Assess fetal heart tones at each visit beginning at 10 to 12 weeks’ gestation.

Fundal height measurement is recommended at each visit during the second and third trimester. There are insufficient data, however, to determine whether this measurement is effective in detecting intrauterine growth restriction.Insufficient evidence also exists to support measurement of fundal height after 36 weeks’ gestation.
Routine cervical examinations are not effective for screening for preterm delivery in low-risk asymptomatic pregnant patients.
Routine screening for edema during pregnancy is not recommended.
Routine urine dipstick testing for glucose and protein have not been proven helpful. Dipstick testing is unreliable in detecting the variable increase in albumin seen with preeclampsia.

If preeclampsia is suspected, investigators in one study found measurement of maternal serum placental growth factor, with <100 pg/mL considered abnormal, was associated with a 2-day faster diagnosis of pre-eclampsia and fewer severe maternal adverse events (4% vs. 5%; adjusted OR 0.32, 95% CI, 0.11-0.96). See the chapter on Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy.

There is insufficient evidence to support use of routine antibiotics during pregnancy to prevent infectious adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes. Although antibiotic prophylaxis given during the second and third trimester reduced the risk of postpartum endometritis, pre-labor rupture of membranes in term pregnancy, and gonococcal infection, there was a high risk of study bias due to small numbers and loss to follow-up. Vaginal antibiotic prophylaxis during pregnancy did not prevent infectious pregnancy outcomes.

The USPSTF recommends against screening for bacterial vaginosis (BV) in pregnant individuals who are not at risk of preterm birth based on no evidence of benefit. The task force also concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against screening for BV in pregnant patients who are at increased risk for preterm delivery. Antibiotics reduced preterm birth in a single trial for a subgroup of patients with a previous preterm birth who had BV. In a recent RCT of patients with confirmed BV, treatment with clindamycin, either twice daily for 4 days or once monthly for 3 months, was no more effective than placebo in preventing a composite outcome of spontaneous late miscarriage (between 16 and 21 weeks') or spontaneous very preterm delivery (between 22 and 32 weeks') for either low-risk patients (0.8%, 1.5% and 1.0%, respectively) or high-risk patients.

Routine measurement of quantitative vaginal fetal fibronectin and serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length at each prenatal visit had low predictive accuracy for spontaneous preterm birth among 9410 nulliparous patients with singleton pregnancies (area under the curve for both tests combined 0.67; 95% CI, 0.64-0.70). Preterm birth occurred in 5%.

It is not known whether fetal movement counting or antenatal cardiotocography (continuous recording of the fetal heart rate via ultrasound) influences pregnancy outcome. In a recent large cohort study, decreased fetal movement in the 3rd trimester was associated with increased incidence of small for gestational age infants. The composite outcome (admission to the NICU, umbilical artery pH <7 or base excess -12 or less, 5-minute APGAR <4, neonatal death or stillbirth) was greater in the decreased fetal movement group. However, the incidence of stillbirth did not differ in this study, likely due to increased obstetric interventions.

Home uterine activity monitoring may result in fewer neonatal intensive care unit admissions but more unscheduled antenatal visits and tocolytic treatment without influencing maternal or perinatal outcomes.
Pregnant patients should be rescreened for anemia at 28 weeks’ gestation. This allows for adequate time to treat anemia if present.
Hemoglobin levels less than 11 g/dL at the initial visit or 10.5 g/dL at 28 weeks’ gestation should be investigated and iron supplementation started, if indicated.

Daily oral iron treatment improves hematological indices but data on reduced risk of low-birth-weight infants is less clear and may depend on the population’s background risk. Authors of another Cochrane review found no data demonstrating important clinical maternal or neonatal effects from oral iron, which causes frequent gastrointestinal adverse effects. If iron side effects are a concern, intermittent (i.e. one, two or three times a week on non-consecutive days) iron or iron plus folic acid regimens produce similar maternal and infant outcomes at birth as daily supplementation.

A recent study performed in sub Saharan Africa showed that 1 dose of 1000 mg ferric carboxymaltose IV for a hemoglobin <10 g/dL was safe but did not reduce anemia prevalence at 36 weeks or increase birth weight.

Repeat screening for atypical red cell antibodies should be done at 28 weeks’ gestation in Rh-negative women. Patients with a negative screen should receive Rho (D) immune globulin while patients with a positive screen should be referred for further workup for Rh hemolytic disease. Administration of 100 µg (500 IU) anti-D to patients in their first pregnancy is believed to reduce the risk of Rhesus D alloimmunization during or immediately after a first pregnancy from 1% to about 0.2% with no adverse effects. Trial data to support this supposition, however, are lacking and Cochrane authors found no data on the risk of Rhesus D alloimmunization in a subsequent pregnancy.

In the US, the CDC reports that the rate of early-onset group B strep infection has decreased from 1.7 cases per 1,000 live births in 1993 to 0.22 cases per 1,000 live births in 2016 with prevention efforts.

The CDC along with ACOG, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians recommend screening all pregnant patients at 35 to 37 weeks gestation using a vaginal-rectal culture to identify women colonized with GBS.
summarizes the indications for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS.

The antibiotic of choice is penicillin or ampicillin. If a severe penicillin allergy is present, sensitivities for clindamycin and erythromycin should be conducted, otherwise cefazolin should be used. If GBS is resistant to clindamycin, then treatment with vancomycin is indicated.

Multiple reviews have been done to study the effect of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) on early-onset GBS disease (EOGBS) and found that increased rates of IAP coverage is linearly associated with reduced risk of EOGBS.

algorithm.title: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for group B streptococcus (GBS)

cell.label: Positive GBS culture at 35-37 weeks' gestation. Penicillin allergic?
GBS resistant to clindamycin or erythromycin, or sensitivity unknown?
Penicillin G 5 million U load, then 2.5 million U every 4 hours, OR ampicillin 2 g IV load, then 1 g IV every 4 hours until delivery.
Cefazolin 2 g IV initial dose, then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery.
Vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours until delivery.
Check sensitivities and start clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours until delivery OR erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours until delivery.
